::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .92", "p = .15"), Sentence = c("However, no individual edge differences remained significant following correction for multiple comparisons, and no sex differences were observed in global network strength (S = .08, p = .92).", "In contrast, no significant differences in network structure were observed between adolescents younger than 14 years and those aged 14 years or older (M = .23, p = .15)." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Adolescence is a critical period for the emergence of emotional and behavioural difficulties, with approximately half of all lifetime mental disorders developing before age 18 (Solmi et al., 2022).

text.text: At the same time, adolescents face increasing emotional, social, and interpersonal demands, making affect regulation particularly important for healthy adjustment (Sisk & Gee, 2022).

text.text: Among the factors that promote resilience during this developmental period, secure attachment relationships have consistently been associated with better emotional, social, and behavioural functioning (Godor et al., 2024; Malik et al., 2021; Sancho et al., 2025).

text.text: Attachment theory proposes that repeated interactions with caregivers shape internal working models, or expectations regarding the availability and responsiveness of others that guide how individuals interpret social experiences, seek support, and respond to distress (Allen & Tan, 2016; Godor et al., 2024; Mikulincer & Shaver, 2007).

text.text: Increasingly, researchers have identified affect regulation as a key mechanism through which these attachment-related expectations influence adjustment and risk for psychopathology (Eilert & Buchheim, 2023; Lewczuk et al., 2021; Pascuzzo et al., 2015; Salavou et al., 2026; Shao et al., 2022).

text.text: Consistent with this perspective, attachment insecurity has been linked to difficulties understanding, managing, and responding to emotional experiences, as well as elevated symptoms of anxiety, depression, and behavioural concerns (Chan et al., 2023; Vernon & Moretti, 2024; Wang et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Consistent with this perspective, attachment insecurity has been linked to difficulties understanding, managing, and responding to emotional experiences, as well as elevated symptoms of anxiety, depression, and behavioural concerns <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Chan et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Vernon & Moretti, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Wang et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Despite strong theoretical and empirical support for the connection between attachment and affect regulation, research has predominantly examined these constructs at the level of broad attachment dimensions and affect regulation processes rather than individual experiences and beliefs.
Consequently, relatively little is known about how specific attachment experiences and affect regulation processes are organized and interconnected.
For example, fears of abandonment, reluctance to seek support, emotional suppression, and beliefs about emotions may each play distinct roles in adolescent adjustment.
Examining how these experiences relate to one another may provide a more nuanced understanding of the processes linking attachment insecurity and affect regulation difficulties during adolescence.

Network theory provides a useful framework for investigating these questions by conceptualizing psychological phenomena as systems of mutually interacting experiences, beliefs, emotions, and behaviours (Schmittmann et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Network theory provides a useful framework for investigating these questions by conceptualizing psychological phenomena as systems of mutually interacting experiences, beliefs, emotions, and behaviours <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Schmittmann et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Within this framework, attachment and affect regulation can be understood as interconnected systems in which specific attachment-related expectations and regulatory processes co-occur and reinforce one another.

Rather than focusing exclusively on broad dimensions of attachment insecurity or affect regulation, network approaches allow researchers to identify which individual experiences are most strongly interconnected and which may serve as bridges linking different psychological domains.
Recent network studies have begun to apply this approach to attachment, affect, and emotion regulation.

In adult samples, network analyses have demonstrated that attachment insecurity is closely intertwined with emotion regulation difficulties and psychopathology, with maladaptive regulatory strategies such as expressive suppression and rumination emerging as important bridge processes linking attachment-related experiences to symptoms of psychological distress (Fuchshuber et al., 2024; Zou et al., 2024).

text.text: Similarly, adolescent network studies have identified attachment-related experiences as central features within broader networks of anxiety, self-injury, childhood trauma, peer relationships, and family functioning (Dong et al., 2025; Joss et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2024).

text.text: Collectively, these findings support the view that attachment is embedded within broader socioemotional systems and is closely linked to emotion regulation and mental health outcomes.

However, despite growing interest in network approaches to attachment and emotion regulation, relatively little research has examined how parentadolescent attachment and affect regulation processes are jointly organized at the level of specific experiences within clinical adolescent populations.

This represents an important area for investigation given theoretical models positioning attachment relationships as central contexts for the development and organization of affect regulation and psychopathology during adolescence (Allen & Tan, 2016; Gross & Cassidy, 2019).

text.text: The present study examined the organization of attachment-related experiences and affect regulation processes within a clinical sample of adolescents.
Using network analysis, we investigated how specific attachment and affect regulation experiences clustered together and interconnected at the item level.

Particular attention was given to identifying bridge indicators linking attachment insecurity and affect regulation, as these experiences may provide insight into how attachment-related vulnerabilities are associated with adolescent emotional and behavioural difficulties.

Based on previous research linking attachment anxiety with heightened emotional reactivity and attachment avoidance with emotional suppression (Brenning et al., 2012; Gross & Cassidy, 2019), we hypothesized that attachment anxiety would be more closely associated with affect dysregulation, whereas attachment avoidance would be more closely associated with affect suppression.

text.text: We also explored whether the structure of the attachment-affect regulation network differed across age and sex.

text.text: The Affect Regulation Checklist (ARC, Moretti, 2003) is a 12-item measure designed to assess affect regulation in youth with a 5-point Likert scale.
text.formatted: The Affect Regulation Checklist (ARC, <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Moretti, 2003)</ref> is a 12-item measure designed to assess affect regulation in youth with a 5-point Likert scale.

text.text: This measure is structured around three core dimensions: (1) affect dysregulation (4 items; e.g., "I have a hard time controlling my feelings"), (2) affect suppression (4 items; e.g., "I try hard not to think about my feelings"), and (3) affect reflection (4 items; e.g., "Thinking about why I have different feelings helps me to learn about myself").
Importantly, the ARC was intentionally designed to assess general responses to affective arousal, avoiding references to specific emotions.
Within this framework, affect dysregulation refers to the inability to engage in adaptive regulation strategies when confronted with intense emotional experiences.

Affect suppression denotes efforts to avoid, control, or distract oneself from these strong affective states, whereas affect reflection involves a cognitive process of stepping back to consider one's emotional experiences and their underlying causes.

The ARC has been empirically validated, demonstrating robust psychometric properties, including high internal consistency (Ames et al., 2022; Benzi et al., 2023; Brown et al., 2021; Craig et al., 2022; Moretti et al., 2015), as well as strong construct and structural validity (Goulter et al., 2022; Vernon & Moretti, 2024).

text.text: Community detection analyses identified four distinct clusters corresponding to: (1) attachment anxiety, (2) attachment avoidance, (3) affect dysregulation and suppression, and (4) affect reflection.

Two nodes emerged as bridges (Figure 2) connecting the attachment and affect regulation communities: R4 ("Thinking about my feelings just makes everything worse") and Av6 ("I want to get close to my parent, but I keep pulling back").

text.text: Specifically, Av6 connected the attachment avoidance cluster with both attachment anxiety and dysregulation/suppression nodes (w(Av6, Ax5) = .27; w(Av6, Av2) = .11; w(Av6, S1) = .08; w(Av6, D4) = .07).
Similarly, R4 connected the reflection cluster with attachment avoidance through Av2 (w(R4, Av2) = .06).
Together, these findings suggest that R4 and Av6 serve as key links between attachmentrelated experiences and affect regulation processes.

The present study examined how attachment-related experiences and affect regulation processes are organized among adolescents with mental health concerns.
While attachment anxiety, attachment avoidance, affect dysregulation/suppression, and affect reflection emerged as distinct communities, they did not operate in isolation.

Instead, the network was anchored by two key experiences: believing that thinking about one's feelings makes things worse and wanting closeness with attachment figures while simultaneously pulling away from it.

These findings highlight beliefs about emotions and uncertainty regarding interpersonal closeness as important points of connection between attachment insecurity and affect regulation difficulties during adolescence.
The broader network structure provides additional insight into how these experiences are organized and interconnected.

The finding that attachment anxiety and attachment avoidance emerged as separate communities aligns with attachment theory's view of anxiety and avoidance as distinct patterns of expectations regarding caregiver availability and responsiveness (Allen & Tan, 2016).
text.formatted: The finding that attachment anxiety and attachment avoidance emerged as separate communities aligns with attachment theory's view of anxiety and avoidance as distinct patterns of expectations regarding caregiver availability and responsiveness <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Allen & Tan, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, affect dysregulation and suppression formed a single community when examined alongside attachment dimensions.

This pattern suggests that, among adolescents experiencing mental health concerns, becoming overwhelmed by emotional experiences and attempting to suppress those experiences may function as closely interconnected aspects of emotional functioning.

These findings are consistent with contemporary perspectives that conceptualize emotion regulation difficulties as involving interacting patterns of emotional reactivity, avoidance, and suppression rather than discrete regulatory styles (Cole et al., 2019; Gross & Cassidy, 2019; Lougheed & Keskin, 2021).
text.formatted: These findings are consistent with contemporary perspectives that conceptualize emotion regulation difficulties as involving interacting patterns of emotional reactivity, avoidance, and suppression rather than discrete regulatory styles <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Cole et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Gross & Cassidy, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Lougheed & Keskin, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Notably, the affect reflection items were not closely connected to the dysregulation and suppression community, suggesting that adolescents' self-reported tendency to reflect on their feelings, behaviour, and life experiences to gain self-understanding represents a distinct aspect of emotional functioning.
Because these findings were based on adolescents' own reports, they reflect youths' awareness of engaging in self-reflective processes rather than the quality or effectiveness of those processes.

This distinction may be important, as developmental models increasingly recognize that awareness of one's emotional experiences and the capacity to regulate those experiences are related but distinct components of emotional functioning (Lougheed et al., 2020; Nook et al., 2021).
text.formatted: This distinction may be important, as developmental models increasingly recognize that awareness of one's emotional experiences and the capacity to regulate those experiences are related but distinct components of emotional functioning <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Lougheed et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Nook et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, adolescents who perceive themselves as engaging in self-reflection may nonetheless experience significant difficulties managing or avoiding their emotions.

One interpretation is that self-reflection facilitates emotional awareness and self-understanding, but does not, on its own, ensure the flexible and effective regulation of emotional experiences (Gross et al., 2019; Lougheed & Keskin, 2021).
text.formatted: One interpretation is that self-reflection facilitates emotional awareness and self-understanding, but does not, on its own, ensure the flexible and effective regulation of emotional experiences <ref type="bibr">(Gross et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Lougheed & Keskin, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The separation of the reflection community from the dysregulation/suppression community therefore suggests that emotional awareness and emotional regulation should not be assumed to reflect a single underlying process.
Rather, adolescents may report engaging in self-reflection while simultaneously experiencing substantial difficulties regulating their emotional experiences.
Age-related analyses revealed similar network structures across age groups, but stronger overall connectivity among attachment and affect regulation nodes in older adolescents.
Greater network connectivity may therefore reflect increasing integration between attachment-related experiences and emotion regulation processes across adolescence.

Although the present study cannot directly examine this developmental process, the findings suggest that network approaches may provide a useful methodology for investigating how attachment representations become increasingly interconnected with affect regulation over time.
In contrast, evidence for sex differences was limited.

Although an overall difference in network structure was initially observed, no individual edges remained significant following correction for multiple comparisons, and no differences emerged in global strength, suggesting that the overall organization of attachment and affect regulation is largely similar across adolescent males and females in the present sample.
The identification of two bridge nodes highlights the interconnected nature of attachment and affect regulation during adolescence.

Rather than representing isolated attachment or emotion regulation processes, these experiences occupied positions linking the two systems, suggesting that adolescents' emotional experiences are closely embedded within their expectations regarding interpersonal support.
The strongest bridge, R4 ("Thinking about my feelings just makes everything worse"), should not be interpreted simply as reflecting negative beliefs about emotions.
Instead, this item may capture adolescents' broader difficulty making sense of their emotional experiences.

From an attachment perspective, the ability to understand and organize emotional experiences develops within relationships characterized by caregiver availability, emotional responsiveness, and co-regulation (Allen & Tan, 2016; Godor et al., 2024; Mikulincer & Shaver, 2007).

text.text: For adolescents experiencing attachment insecurity, emotional experiences may remain difficult to organize or integrate, leading reflection itself to feel confusing, overwhelming, or unhelpful.

In this context, negative beliefs about emotions may represent one manifestation of a broader difficulty developing coherent meaning from emotional experiences rather than an isolated cognitive belief.

The peripheral position of the broader reflection community alongside the central role of these beliefs may therefore suggest that unsuccessful emotional sense-making, rather than reflection itself, is particularly relevant to the intersection of attachment insecurity and emotion regulation.
The second bridge, Av6 ("I want to get close to my parent, but I keep pulling back"), reflects a complementary relational process.
Adolescence is characterized by increasing autonomy alongside continued reliance on caregivers for emotional security (Allen & Tan, 2016; Kobak et al., 2015).

text.text: For adolescents experiencing mental health difficulties, this developmental transition may become especially complex.

Some adolescents may simultaneously desire parental support while expecting that support to be unavailable, ineffective, or emotionally unsafe based on previous relational experiences (Decarli et al., 2022; Gander et al., 2020).

text.text: Others may resist seeking support because developmental pressures toward autonomy encourage them to manage emotional experiences independently (Babo et al., 2024).

text.text: Consequently, the desire for connection may coexist with withdrawal from available support, reducing opportunities for co-regulation precisely when emotional experiences are most difficult to navigate (Silvers, 2022).

text.text: Taken together, these bridge nodes suggest that attachment insecurity and affect regulation difficulties intersect through adolescents' attempts to understand and manage emotional experiences within the context of attachment relationships.

Rather than identifying isolated intervention targets, the findings highlight interconnected developmental processes whereby difficulties making sense of emotions and uncertainty regarding caregiver availability may mutually reinforce one another.

Attachment insecurity and difficulties with affect regulation are well-established transdiagnostic risk factors for a broad range of emotional and behavioural difficulties (Brenning et al., 2022; Ein-Dor et al., 2016; Klein et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Attachment insecurity and difficulties with affect regulation are well-established transdiagnostic risk factors for a broad range of emotional and behavioural difficulties <ref type="bibr">(Brenning et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Ein-Dor et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Klein et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The present findings suggest that interventions targeting emotion regulation may be most effective when situated within adolescents' relational contexts.

Although interventions that teach emotion regulation skills can improve psychological functioning (Espenes et al., 2024; Moltrecht et al., 2021), the current network suggests that difficulties regulating emotion may not arise solely from deficits in regulatory skills.
text.formatted: Although interventions that teach emotion regulation skills can improve psychological functioning <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Espenes et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Moltrecht et al., 2021)</ref>, the current network suggests that difficulties regulating emotion may not arise solely from deficits in regulatory skills.

text.text: Rather, emotion regulation difficulties appear closely intertwined with adolescents' experiences of attachment relationships, including uncertainty regarding caregiver availability and difficulty making coherent sense of emotional experiences.

This interpretation complements research demonstrating that beliefs about emotions and their perceived controllability are associated with emotion regulation strategies and psychopathology (Becerra et al., 2024; Deplancke et al., 2023; Dickerson et al., 2018; Ford et al., 2018; Ford & Gross, 2019; Ge et al., 2024; Somerville et al., 2024), while suggesting that these beliefs may themselves be shaped within relational contexts.

text.text: Accordingly, interventions that simultaneously strengthen caregiver-adolescent relationships while promoting emotional understanding, reflective functioning, and co-regulation may be particularly well positioned to address the interconnected processes identified in the present network.

At the relational level, attachment-based parenting interventions have shown promise for reducing adolescent attachment insecurity, behavioural problems, and parent-child affect dysregulation (Moretti et al., 2015; Vernon & Moretti, under review).
text.formatted: At the relational level, attachment-based parenting interventions have shown promise for reducing adolescent attachment insecurity, behavioural problems, and parent-child affect dysregulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Moretti et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Vernon & Moretti, under review)</ref>.

text.text: The present findings may help refine this intervention focus by highlighting the importance of caregiver emotional availability, particularly when adolescents experience uncertainty about seeking support.

As adolescents seek greater independence, caregivers continue to serve as important sources of security and co-regulation, even when support needs are not communicated directly (Allen & Tan, 2016; Kobak et al., 2015).
text.formatted: As adolescents seek greater independence, caregivers continue to serve as important sources of security and co-regulation, even when support needs are not communicated directly <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Allen & Tan, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Kobak et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Interventions that support caregivers in remaining emotionally accessible and responsive, while helping adolescents build confidence in the availability of support, may be especially relevant for addressing the attachment-affect regulation processes identified in the current network.
Several limitations should be considered when interpreting the present findings.
First, the crosssectional design precludes conclusions regarding the directionality of associations among attachmentrelated experiences and affect regulation processes.

Longitudinal research is needed to determine whether the bridge processes identified in the current study represent developmental pathways through which attachment insecurity contributes to subsequent emotional and behavioural difficulties.
Second, all variables were assessed using adolescent self-report measures.

Although self-report provides valuable insight into youths' subjective experiences, future research would benefit from simultaneously examining caregiver and adolescent perceptions of attachment and emotion regulation using multiple methodologies, including observational paradigms, interview-based assessments, and caregiver-and youth-report measures.

Examining these processes across multiple levels of analysis would provide a more comprehensive understanding of how adolescents' emotional experiences are shaped within attachment relationships and how caregiver and adolescent regulatory processes interact over time.
Third, the sample consisted exclusively of adolescents referred for mental health or behavioural concerns.

While this clinical sample provided a valuable opportunity to examine attachment-related affect regulation among youth at elevated risk for emotional difficulties, the findings may not generalize to community populations.

Future studies should compare attachment-affect regulation networks across clinical and non-clinical samples to determine whether the observed network structure and bridge processes are unique to adolescents experiencing mental health concerns.
Finally, self-reported biological sex, rather than gender identity, was examined using a binary categorization of male and female participants.

As sex and gender are distinct constructs, the present findings cannot be generalized to gender-diverse adolescents, whose attachment experiences, emotion regulation processes, and mental health outcomes differ in important ways (Caldarera et al., 2022; Mezzalira et al., 2022).

text.text: Future research should adopt more inclusive approaches to assessing gender identity and examine whether the organization of attachment and affect regulation differs across diverse gender groups.
Despite these limitations, the present study demonstrates the value of network approaches for investigating attachment-related affect regulation during adolescence.
This study examined the organization of attachment-related experiences and affect regulation processes within a clinical sample of adolescents.
Attachment anxiety and attachment avoidance emerged as distinct dimensions of insecurity, whereas affect dysregulation and suppression formed a unified regulatory community.

Most notably, negative beliefs about emotional reflection and conflicting feelings regarding closeness to caregivers emerged as key bridge processes linking attachment insecurity with affect regulation difficulties.

These findings support perspectives that conceptualize attachment relationships as central contexts for affect regulation and highlight beliefs about emotions and interpersonal support as key features of the attachment-affect regulation network among adolescents with mental health concerns.
